title: Celexa and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Citalopram?
excerpt: Can you drink on Celexa? What the citalopram label says, its heart rhythm warning, why you may get drunk faster, skipping doses, and when it turns risky.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Celexa (citalopram)? What the label says, the heart rhythm warning, feeling drunk faster, skipping doses, and when it gets risky.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the official guidance is that you shouldn't drink alcohol while taking Celexa (citalopram). The US prescribing information says that although Celexa didn't make alcohol's effects on thinking and coordination worse in a clinical trial, alcohol use by depressed patients taking Celexa is not recommended. For most people who are stable on a normal dose, an occasional light drink is not dangerous in the way mixing alcohol with opioids or sleeping pills can be, and many doctors are comfortable with it. But citalopram has one feature that sets it apart from most other antidepressants: a dose-related effect on the heart's rhythm. Heavy drinking can push in the same direction, which is why binge drinking on Celexa deserves more caution than a glass of wine with dinner.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink in the first few weeks of treatment or right after a dose change. Don't skip doses so you can drink. Expect your old limit to be too much. Avoid binge drinking, especially if you're on 40 mg, over 60, or have any heart condition. Be careful with ibuprofen and aspirin for a hangover. And if drinking makes you feel hopeless or have thoughts of hurting yourself, stop and get help right away.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor.** This article explains general research and the official label for citalopram. It isn't a substitute for the doctor who prescribed your medication, who knows why you take it, what dose you're on, your heart history, and what else you take. **Talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before drinking on Celexa if** you've just started or changed your dose, you take 40 mg a day or you're over 60, you have a heart condition or have been told you have a long QT interval, you take other medicines that affect the brain or the heart, or you have a history of heavy drinking. **Get help immediately if** you have thoughts of suicide or self-harm: in the US, call or text **988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) or call 911. Also get emergency care if after drinking you faint, have a pounding or irregular heartbeat with dizziness, have a seizure, or have a fast heartbeat with fever, agitation, muscle twitching, or confusion.

## How Celexa and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Celexa is the brand name for **citalopram**, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). In the US it's approved for depression, and doctors also commonly prescribe it for anxiety and related conditions. It works by keeping more serotonin, one of the brain's chemical messengers, available between nerve cells. The effect builds over several weeks, which is why it doesn't help on day one.

Alcohol and citalopram don't clash in the liver the way alcohol and acetaminophen do. Citalopram is broken down mainly by liver enzymes called CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6, and moderate drinking doesn't meaningfully change that process. So the main problem isn't that one drug makes the other build up to toxic levels.

The interaction happens in two places: the brain and, less commonly, the heart.

1. **Both act on the central nervous system.** Alcohol is a depressant. It slows brain activity, mostly by boosting the calming GABA system and blocking the excitatory glutamate system. Citalopram changes serotonin signaling, and common side effects include drowsiness, tiredness, and dizziness. Add alcohol and those effects can stack, so you can feel more sedated, unsteady, or foggy than either would cause alone.
2. **Alcohol pushes mood the other way.** Citalopram is trying to lift and steady your mood over weeks. Alcohol gives a short lift followed by a dip, and regular heavy drinking is linked to more depression and anxiety over time. The two work against each other.
3. **Alcohol disrupts sleep.** It helps you fall asleep but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Poor sleep is one of the strongest drivers of low mood and anxiety.
4. **Both can affect heart rhythm.** This is the part that's specific to citalopram, and it gets its own section below.

### What the official label says, and why it sounds mixed

The Celexa prescribing information says that in a clinical trial, citalopram did not make alcohol's effects on cognitive and motor skills (things like reaction time and coordination) worse. Then it says that, as with other psychiatric medications, alcohol use by depressed patients taking Celexa is not recommended.

Those statements fit together. The trial asked a narrow question in a controlled setting: does the drug make a measured dose of alcohol impair you more? The recommendation covers the bigger picture. Alcohol can worsen the depression citalopram treats, people react differently, and some situations (early treatment, high doses, other medicines, heavy drinking) carry more risk. "Not recommended" is not the same as "dangerous in any amount," but it's not a green light either.

## The Heart Rhythm Warning: Why Celexa Is Different

If you've read about other SSRIs and alcohol, most of the advice carries over to Celexa. The one big difference is the heart.

Every heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the heart muscle needs a moment to "reset" before the next one. On an electrocardiogram (ECG), part of that reset time is measured as the **QT interval**. When the QT interval gets too long, the heart becomes more prone to a dangerous, chaotic rhythm called torsades de pointes, which can cause fainting and, rarely, sudden death.

Citalopram lengthens the QT interval in a dose-dependent way, meaning the higher the dose, the bigger the effect. In 2011 the FDA issued a safety communication saying citalopram should no longer be prescribed at doses above 40 mg a day, because higher doses didn't add meaningful benefit for depression but did increase the effect on heart rhythm. The FDA also advised a maximum of 20 mg a day for people over 60, people with liver problems, people whose bodies break down citalopram slowly (called CYP2C19 poor metabolizers), and people taking certain medicines that raise citalopram levels. The label advises caution, or avoiding citalopram, in people with congenital long QT syndrome, recent heart attack, heart failure, or slow heart rate, and recommends correcting low potassium or low magnesium.

For a healthy person on 20 mg, the QT effect is usually small and not something they'd ever notice. Escitalopram (Lexapro), which is closely related, has a similar but generally smaller effect. Most other common SSRIs, such as sertraline, have less of a reputation for it.

### Where alcohol comes in

Moderate drinking isn't known to meaningfully change citalopram's effect on the heart. Heavy drinking is a different story, for several reasons that can add up:

- **Vomiting and diarrhea drain potassium and magnesium.** A rough night that ends with being sick, followed by a day of not eating much, can leave you low on both minerals. Low potassium and low magnesium are well-known risk factors for QT prolongation and rhythm problems, and the Celexa label specifically mentions them.
- **Binge drinking itself can upset heart rhythm.** Doctors have long recognized that heavy drinking sessions can trigger irregular heartbeats in otherwise healthy people, sometimes called "holiday heart." Heavy drinking and alcohol withdrawal have also been linked to a longer QT interval.
- **Dehydration and a racing heart.** A hangover often comes with a faster heart rate and feeling lightheaded. Usually that's harmless, but it's not the state you want your heart in if its rhythm is already being nudged.
- **Mixing in other QT-prolonging medicines.** Some anti-nausea drugs (like ondansetron), certain antibiotics, some antihistamines in higher doses, and other medicines can add to the effect. People sometimes reach for these when they're sick after drinking.

None of this means one drink is a heart risk on Celexa. It means the combination that deserves respect is **heavy drinking plus vomiting plus a higher dose or an existing heart issue.** If that describes your situation, it's a conversation worth having with your doctor before you drink, not after.

If your heart races after drinking even off medication, our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains the common causes and which signs need a doctor.

## Citalopram and Alcohol: Same Drug, Same Advice

Citalopram is the generic name for Celexa, and the generic is what most people actually take. Everything on this page applies equally to brand-name Celexa and generic citalopram tablets or liquid. The active ingredient is the same, the label warnings are the same, and pharmacists treat them as interchangeable.

You may also see citalopram compared with **escitalopram (Lexapro)**. Citalopram is a mix of two mirror-image forms of the same molecule. Escitalopram is just the active one of those two forms, so it's prescribed at lower doses. The alcohol advice for the two is very similar, with the heart rhythm limits being stricter for citalopram. If you've switched between them, see our separate page on [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol). For how the main antidepressant classes compare, see [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol).

## Why You Might Feel Drunker Faster on Celexa

Many people report getting drunk faster after starting citalopram, or blacking out on an amount that used to be fine. It's one of the most common things people search for, so it deserves a straight answer.

**Celexa doesn't raise your blood alcohol.** Two drinks give you roughly the same blood alcohol level on citalopram as off it, and the trial in the label didn't find extra impairment on its tests.

**But feeling it more is real for a lot of people.** Some likely reasons:

- **Stacked side effects.** If citalopram already makes you a little drowsy or lightheaded, especially early on or after a dose increase, alcohol adds to that. You feel more impaired at the same blood alcohol level.
- **Individual variation.** Trials report averages. Some people respond much more strongly to the combination.
- **Lower tolerance than you think.** People who have been depressed often drank less, ate irregularly, or stopped going out. When the medication starts working and they go out again, they drink at their old pace and overshoot.
- **Less anxiety, fewer brakes.** If worry used to keep you cautious, feeling more relaxed can make it easier to keep drinking past your plan.

### Blackouts on Celexa

A blackout is a gap in memory caused by alcohol blocking the brain from saving new memories. It happens when blood alcohol rises quickly, usually from drinking fast or on an empty stomach. There's no good evidence that citalopram directly causes blackouts. But if you feel the drinks more, lose track of how many you've had, or drink faster because you feel relaxed, you're more likely to reach the levels where blackouts happen. If you've blacked out on Celexa, take it as a sign to cut back sharply, and mention it to your prescriber.

The practical rule: **assume your old limit no longer applies.** The first few times you drink on Celexa, have one drink, eat, wait, and see how you feel. Don't drive, and don't be the person responsible for anyone else that night.

## Celexa and Drinking: How Much Is Too Much?

There's no official safe amount, because the label recommends not drinking. What follows is general context to bring to your doctor, not a personal limit.

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| First 2 to 4 weeks, or right after a dose change | Best to avoid alcohol until you know how the medication affects you. Side effects are usually strongest early on. |
| Stable on 10 to 20 mg, healthy heart, occasional light drinking | Many prescribers consider one drink now and then acceptable for some patients. Ask yours. Drink slowly and eat. |
| On 40 mg, over 60, or any heart condition | Talk to your doctor before drinking at all. Heavy drinking and vomiting are worth avoiding entirely. |
| Binge drinking (4+ drinks for women, 5+ for men in about two hours) | Not a good idea on Celexa. It raises the odds of heavy sedation, poor decisions, a mood crash, vomiting, and mineral losses that matter for heart rhythm. |
| Drinking most days, or using alcohol to cope with low mood | Tell your prescriber. This pattern tends to keep depression going and can stop the medication from helping. |
| Taking other sedating or heart-rhythm medicines | Ask a pharmacist before drinking at all. |

For reference, US dietary guidance describes moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and two for men, and a standard drink is about 12 oz of regular beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of spirits. Those numbers are for the general population, not for people on an antidepressant. On Celexa, less is the safer direction.

## Should You Skip Your Celexa Dose to Drink?

No, unless your doctor specifically tells you to. People sometimes skip a dose thinking it will "make room" for a night out. It doesn't work, and it can backfire.

- **Citalopram stays in your body a long time.** Its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of it) is about a day and a half. Skipping one dose barely changes the level in your blood that evening.
- **Skipping can cause discontinuation symptoms.** Missing doses or stopping suddenly can bring dizziness, irritability, trouble sleeping, flu-like feelings, and the "brain zaps" some people describe. Those can easily be mistaken for a bad hangover, or make one worse.
- **Stopping and starting undermines treatment.** SSRIs work best at a steady level. Repeatedly missing doses can make depression symptoms come back.

The safer swap is to keep the medication steady and change the drinking: fewer drinks, more food, more water, or a night off.

There's also no point timing drinks around your dose, for example taking citalopram in the morning and drinking at night. Because it's in your system all day once you're on it, the gap between your pill and your drink doesn't make a meaningful difference.

## The Hangover on Celexa: Next-Day Anxiety and Low Mood

The morning after drinking is where a lot of people on Celexa notice the biggest difference.

As alcohol wears off, the brain swings from the calm alcohol created into a rebound state that feels jittery and on edge. Many people call this **hangxiety**. Add in poor sleep, dehydration, and low blood sugar, and you get the familiar mix of dread, guilt, and racing thoughts the next day.

If you take citalopram for depression or anxiety, this rebound can hit harder and feel more personal. It can feel like the medication has stopped working or that you're sliding back. Usually it's the hangover, not a relapse, and it passes within a day or so. But if drinking regularly leaves you low or anxious for several days, that's a sign alcohol is undercutting your treatment.

Ways to soften the next day:

- Drink water before bed and in the morning.
- Eat a real breakfast with some protein and salt.
- Get outside for a short walk if you can.
- Avoid more alcohol to "take the edge off." It delays the crash and can start a cycle.
- If you vomited a lot, sip an electrolyte drink to replace fluids and minerals, which matters more on citalopram.

Our [complete guide to hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) goes deeper into why it happens and what helps.

## Risky Combinations to Know About

Most of the risk with Celexa and alcohol comes from what else is in the mix.

### Other sedating medicines

Sleep aids, benzodiazepines (such as alprazolam or lorazepam), opioid pain medicines, muscle relaxants, gabapentin, and sedating antihistamines all slow the brain. Combined with alcohol and citalopram, the sedation can be strong enough to be dangerous, including slowed breathing in the worst cases. If you take any of these, ask a pharmacist before drinking at all.

### Serotonin syndrome

Serotonin syndrome happens when too much serotonin builds up, usually from combining two or more serotonin-boosting substances. Alcohol alone isn't a typical cause. The risk rises when citalopram is combined with other antidepressants, the migraine drugs called triptans, the pain medicine tramadol, St. John's wort, or recreational drugs like MDMA, which sometimes happens on a night out.

Signs include agitation, confusion, fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, fever, heavy sweating, shivering, muscle twitching or stiffness, and diarrhea. These overlap with being drunk or hungover, which is part of the danger. **If you notice them, get emergency care.**

### Painkillers for the hangover

SSRIs like citalopram affect how blood platelets work, which slightly raises the risk of bleeding. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin) raise the risk of stomach bleeding, and alcohol irritates the stomach lining. The Celexa label warns that combining it with NSAIDs, aspirin, or blood thinners like warfarin increases bleeding risk.

That doesn't mean one ibuprofen is forbidden, but it does mean grabbing painkillers after a night of drinking is less simple on Celexa. Ask a pharmacist which pain reliever suits you. If you use an NSAID, take a single label dose with food and don't use them for days on end. For the trade-offs, see our pages on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol), [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol), and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). Acetaminophen has its own liver warnings with regular heavy drinking.

### Anti-nausea medicines

If you're throwing up after drinking, you might reach for something to settle your stomach. Some anti-nausea medicines, including ondansetron (Zofran), can also lengthen the QT interval. Ask a pharmacist before combining them with citalopram, especially at higher doses.

### Low sodium

SSRIs can occasionally cause low blood sodium (hyponatremia), especially in older adults and people taking water pills. Drinking very large amounts of beer with little food can lower sodium too. It's uncommon, but headache, confusion, weakness, or unsteadiness that seems out of proportion is worth getting checked, particularly if you're older.

### Overdose

Citalopram is more dangerous in overdose than many other SSRIs, partly because of its effect on heart rhythm and its link to seizures at high levels. Alcohol makes any overdose more dangerous. If someone has taken more citalopram than prescribed, with or without alcohol, call 911 or Poison Control (**1-800-222-1222** in the US) right away, even if they seem fine.

## Does Alcohol Make Celexa Less Effective?

Not directly. Alcohol doesn't chemically block citalopram. But it can make the medication look like it isn't working:

- Alcohol is a depressant, and regular heavy use is linked to more depression and anxiety.
- It damages sleep quality, and poor sleep worsens mood.
- Hangovers bring short-term anxiety and low mood that can be mistaken for the medication failing.
- People who drink heavily are more likely to miss doses.

If you're a few months into treatment and don't feel much better, look honestly at how much you're drinking before concluding citalopram doesn't work. Tell your prescriber the real number. Doctors hear this all the time and need accurate information to adjust treatment. Our article on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) explains how the drink-then-worry cycle builds.

## When to See a Doctor

> **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if, while on Celexa and drinking or hungover, you or a friend:**
> - Faint or nearly faint, or have a pounding, fluttering, or irregular heartbeat with dizziness or shortness of breath
> - Have a seizure
> - Have a fast heartbeat with fever, agitation, heavy sweating, muscle twitching or stiffness, or confusion (possible serotonin syndrome)
> - Are very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting while not fully conscious
> - Vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or have black, tarry stools
> - Have thoughts of suicide or self-harm (call or text **988**, or call 911)
>
> **Book a regular appointment with your prescriber if:**
> - You feel much more drunk on Celexa than you expect, or have blacked out
> - You're often anxious or low for days after drinking
> - You're drinking most days or using alcohol to cope
> - You've been vomiting a lot after drinking, especially if you're on 40 mg or have a heart condition
> - You want to know if a different medication would suit your drinking habits better

## Practical Tips If Your Doctor Says an Occasional Drink Is OK

If you've talked it through and your prescriber is comfortable with occasional light drinking, these habits keep the risk low:

1. **Wait until you're settled on the dose.** Avoid alcohol for the first few weeks and after any change.
2. **Start with one drink and wait.** Find out how you react now, not how you reacted before.
3. **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
4. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and helps with next-day dehydration.
5. **Choose lower-strength drinks.** A light beer or a wine spritzer gives you something to hold with less alcohol.
6. **Set a limit before you go out**, and tell a friend.
7. **Don't drive** after drinking, even a small amount.
8. **Avoid mixing** with other substances, especially anything sedating or serotonin-boosting.
9. **Take your Celexa as usual.** Don't skip or double doses.
10. **If you get sick, replace fluids and electrolytes** and take it easy the next day.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

People on Celexa sometimes ask whether a hangover supplement could make drinking easier. Here's an honest view.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it acts on GABA receptors in the brain and may affect how the body handles alcohol. Human data is limited, and **there are no good studies on taking DHM together with citalopram or any SSRI.** Because DHM appears to act on the brain, check with your prescriber or pharmacist before combining it with Celexa. It does not make drinking on an antidepressant safe, it does nothing for the heart rhythm concerns above, and there is no good evidence that it prevents next-day anxiety or low mood.

If your doctor is fine with it and you want to try DHM on the occasional night you do drink, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common medicines, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts.

## Key Takeaways

- The Celexa label says alcohol use is not recommended, even though a trial didn't find it worsened alcohol's effects on coordination.
- Citalopram has a dose-related effect on heart rhythm (the QT interval). Heavy drinking, vomiting, and low potassium or magnesium can add to it.
- Be most careful if you're on 40 mg, over 60, or have a heart condition.
- Many people feel drunk faster on Celexa. Assume your old limit is too much.
- Don't skip doses to drink. Citalopram lasts well over a day in your system.
- Next-day anxiety and low mood can hit harder on an antidepressant.
- Take extra care with sedating medicines, serotonin-boosting substances, NSAID painkillers, and some anti-nausea drugs.
- If drinking ever brings thoughts of suicide or self-harm, stop and get help: call or text 988 in the US.
- The person to ask about your situation is the doctor who prescribed your medication.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I drink alcohol while taking Celexa?**

The official answer is that drinking isn't recommended. The Celexa prescribing information says that although a clinical trial didn't find citalopram made alcohol's effects on thinking and coordination worse, alcohol use by depressed patients taking Celexa is not recommended. Many prescribers are comfortable with an occasional light drink once you're stable on a normal dose and have a healthy heart, but that depends on your dose, age, heart history, other medicines, and drinking habits. Ask the doctor who prescribed it.

**Is citalopram and alcohol the same as Celexa and alcohol?**

Yes. Citalopram is the generic name for Celexa. The active ingredient, the label warnings, and the advice about alcohol are the same whether you take the brand or the generic. Escitalopram (Lexapro) is a closely related but separate medicine with similar alcohol advice and generally a smaller effect on heart rhythm.

**Does drinking on Celexa affect your heart?**

Citalopram can lengthen the QT interval, a measure of the heart's electrical reset time, and the effect grows with dose. That's why the FDA said in 2011 that it shouldn't be prescribed above 40 mg a day, and above 20 mg a day for people over 60. Moderate drinking isn't known to change this much, but heavy drinking, vomiting, and the low potassium and magnesium that can follow can add to the risk of rhythm problems. If you faint or have a pounding or irregular heartbeat with dizziness, get emergency care.

**Why do I get drunk faster on Celexa?**

Celexa doesn't make your blood alcohol rise faster. But many people feel the drinks more, especially early in treatment or after a dose increase, because citalopram's side effects such as drowsiness and dizziness can stack with alcohol's. Lower tolerance and feeling more relaxed can also lead to drinking faster than you used to. Treat your old limit as no longer reliable: drink slower, eat first, and have less.

**Should I skip my Celexa dose if I'm going to drink?**

No, not unless your doctor tells you to. Citalopram has a half-life of about a day and a half, so skipping one dose won't clear it before a night out. Missing doses can cause discontinuation symptoms such as dizziness, irritability, and flu-like feelings, and stopping and starting can undermine treatment. Take it as prescribed and adjust the drinking instead.

**How long after taking Celexa can I drink?**

There's no safe waiting window. Once you're on citalopram it's in your system all day, every day, so timing a drink a few hours after your pill doesn't change much. The more useful questions are how much you drink, how you feel on the medication, your dose, and what your doctor says about your situation.

**Can alcohol make Celexa stop working?**

Alcohol doesn't chemically block citalopram, but it can work against it. Regular or heavy drinking is linked to worse depression and anxiety, poorer sleep, and low mood in the days after drinking, and people who drink heavily are more likely to miss doses. If you feel Celexa isn't working, tell your doctor honestly how much you drink.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover while on Celexa?**

Be careful. SSRIs like citalopram can raise bleeding risk, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin raise the risk of stomach bleeding, especially after alcohol. The Celexa label warns about combining it with NSAIDs, aspirin, and blood thinners. Ask a pharmacist which pain reliever suits you, and if you use an NSAID, take a single label dose with food.

**Can I take DHM while on Celexa?**

Check with your doctor or pharmacist first. DHM is a plant compound that lab and animal research suggests acts on GABA receptors in the brain, and there are no good human studies on combining it with citalopram. It isn't a way to make drinking on an antidepressant safe and does nothing for citalopram's heart rhythm effect. If your prescriber is fine with it, follow the product label.
